items.prompt: Finish reverse_tr, a tail-recursive version of the non-tail-recursive reverse. It must give the same results and use bounded stack space. No standard library functions, including @.
items.key:
let reverse_tr (l : 'a list) : 'a list =
  let rec loop (m : 'a list) (acc : 'a list) : 'a list =
    begin match m with
    | [] -> acc
    | hd :: tl -> loop tl (hd :: acc)
    end
  in loop l []

items.prompt: Rewrite transform (map) so it is tail recursive, with the same results and constant stack use. Helpers you define yourself are allowed; standard library functions are not.
items.code:
let rec transform (f : 'a -> 'b) (l : 'a list) : 'b list =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> []
  | x :: xs -> f x :: transform f xs
  end

let transform_tr (f : 'a -> 'b) (l : 'a list) : 'b list =
  ____
items.key:
let transform_tr (f : 'a -> 'b) (l : 'a list) : 'b list =
  let rec loop (acc : 'b list) (rest : 'a list) : 'b list =
    begin match rest with
    | [] -> reverse_tr acc
    | hd :: tl -> loop (f hd :: acc) tl
    end
  in loop [] l
items.notes: The official solution calls reverse_tr from 1.1, which counts as a helper you defined yourself.

items.prompt: Draw the stack and heap after merge d1 d2. The BEFORE picture shows d1 as [18; 9] (head is the 18 node, tail is the 9 node) and d2 as [102; 64], with prev/next links in both directions. Add the arrows and Some blobs for the AFTER state; the four nodes and the two deque records are already drawn.
items.key: d1 = [18; 9; 102; 64]: d1.head -> Some 18-node, d1.tail -> Some 64-node. 9.next -> Some 102-node and 102.prev -> Some 9-node; every other link is unchanged. d2.head and d2.tail are both None.

items.prompt: Fill in merge so it appends all of d2's nodes to the end of d1 and leaves d2 empty. Handle the cases where d2 is empty, where d1 is empty, and where both are non-empty.
items.key:
let merge (d1 : 'a deque) (d2 : 'a deque) : unit =
  begin match d2.head with
  | None -> ()
  | Some n ->
    begin match d1.tail with
    | None ->
      d1.head <- d2.head; d1.tail <- d2.tail;
      d2.head <- None; d2.tail <- None
    | Some m ->
      m.next <- d2.head; n.prev <- d1.tail;
      d1.tail <- d2.tail;
      d2.head <- None; d2.tail <- None
    end
  end
items.notes: The skeleton already has the two valid checks at the top. The exam's ((d2: 'a deque)) has an extra, harmless pair of parentheses.

items.prompt: Finish a property-based test: given op lists ops1 and ops2 that build d1 and d2, merge them, then check that d1 holds the concatenation and d2 is empty. Library functions such as @ are allowed.
items.code:
let property ((ops1, ops2) : int op list * int op list) : bool =
  let d1 : int deque = init_with ops1 in
  let d2 : int deque = init_with ops2 in
  let l1 = to_list d1 in
  let l2 = to_list d2 in
  (* Fill in here... *)
items.key:
merge d1 d2;
to_list d1 = l1 @ l2
items.notes: The official answer only checks the concatenation. The prompt also says d2 becomes empty, so adding && to_list d2 = [] is a stricter, also-correct answer.

items.prompt: Write code that builds the pictured stack and heap. p1 points to node {v=1}, whose next is Some of the node p2 points to ({v=3}). That node's next is Some of p3's node ({v=5}), and the 5 node's next points back to Some of the 3 node, forming a cycle.
items.notes: The exam doesn't number a subpart here; 3.1 is our label for the whole 5-point question. p1.next <- p3.next reuses the Some cell from p3.next, so p1 and p3 share one Some p2 cell, as in the picture.

items.prompt: Implement isLocalPeak and countLocalPeaks for an n x n grid of positive ints. A local peak is strictly greater than every existing up/down/left/right neighbor. Examples: [[10,12,11],[9,20,15],[8,14,13]] gives 1, and [[50,30,5],[10,12,8],[2,4,25]] gives 2.

Explain in English how to change your solution so it works when the grid is rectangular or jagged (rows of different lengths). In the example jagged grid, rows are [1,1,1,2], [1,2], [2,1,1,3] and [1,2,1,3,1,1], and the answer is 4.
items.key: Add a helper lookup(grid, r, c) that returns -1 when (r, c) is out of bounds (check 0 <= r < grid.length and 0 <= c < grid[r].length), and the cell value otherwise. Compare each cell against lookup of its four neighbors; since all values are positive, -1 never blocks a peak. In countLocalPeaks, loop c from 0 to grid[r].length instead of n.
items.notes: The official answer says r > grid.length and c > grid[r].length; the correct out-of-bounds tests are >=. Checked on the example: peaks at (0,3), (1,1), (2,0) and (3,1) give 4.
